blocks.text: Chrysippus admires this so much that he asserts τὸ ζῶον γεγονέναι ἕνεκα τῆς κέρκου, καὶ οὐκ ἀνάπαλιν [to zōon gegonenai heneka tēs kerkou, kai ouk anapalin], that this animal was created for the sake of its tail, and not the reverse, that is, the tail for the sake of the animal. So Plutarch in the book De Stoicorum contrar. Accordingly, to show itself off, it spreads not its wings but its tail. Pliny: At the same time it seeks with its tail curved like a shell certain reflections of shade for the other feathers, which gleam more brightly in the dark. Columella: It covers itself, as if admiring itself, with the jewelled feathers of its tail. Dio Chrysostom: Ἀνακλάσας ^{g)} τὴν οὐρὰν, καὶ περιστήσας αὐτῷ πανταχόθεν ὥσπερ εὐειδὲς θέατρον [Anaklasas tēn ouran, kai peristēsas autō pantachothen hōsper eueides theatron]. Bending back its tail, and setting it up all around itself like a handsome theatre. Phaedrus, book 3, Fable 57:
And unfolding its jewelled tail with painted plumage.

Lucian: Τὴν οὐρὰν ἐπάρας, καὶ πάντοθεν αὐτῷ περιστήσας, ἐπιδείκνυται τὰ ἄνθη τὰ αὐτοῦ [Tēn ouran eparas, kai pantothen autō peristēsas, epideiknytai ta anthē ta autou]; With its tail raised and spread all around, it also displays its flowers. The Etymologicum: Τοῖς ὁρῶσι τὴν οὐρὰν ἑξαπλοῦν ἀποδεικνύει [Tois horōsi tēn ouran hexaploun apodeiknyei]. It displays its sixfold tail to the onlookers. Damir: عقد ذنبه كالطاقة [ʿaqada dhanabahu ka-l-ṭāqa] It arranges its tail like an arched work. Hence it is that with the tail the peacock's whole glory perishes. Pliny: Therefore, when its tail is lost each year together with the leaves of the trees, until it grows again with the blossom, it seeks a hiding place, ashamed and mournful. I am not unaware that the poets attribute to the wings, καταχρηστικῶς [katachrēstikōs], what belongs properly to the tail. Moschus:
Ὄρνις ἀγαλλόμενος πτερύγων πολυανθέϊ χροίῃ, [Ornis agallomenos pterygōn polyanthei chroiē,]
A bird exulting in the flowery colour of its wings. Martial in the Xenia, Epigram 70:
You marvel whenever it unfolds its jewelled wings.

The patrician fans himself with rosy peacocks' wings. [II, 847] With peacocks' wings, that is, tails. For fans of this kind were made from the peacock's tail. Martial in the Apophoreta, on a peacock fly-whisk:
That which keeps the foul flies from licking your meal was the proud tail of a splendid bird.
And now fans from the proud peacock's tail.

But in Scripture כנף, in a bird, signifies nothing other than the wing. Therefore רננים [col. 245] renanim must be birds that truly exult in their wings, or that have in their wings some ground for exulting.

That these are ostriches, many things not only suggest but prove. 1. The authority of Jerome, who rendered it so; no such authority is brought forward by those who understand peacocks here. 2. Just as the two verbs ענה ana and רנן ranan are entirely synonymous in the sense of crying out and singing, so it is credible that the two bird names derived from them, which are moreover of almost the same form, are synonymous: namely יענים jeenim and רננים renanim. Therefore, as יענים means female ostriches, as we proved above ^{b)}, so too does רננים. These, moreover, are so named διακριτικῶς [diakritikōs], because, while the voice of the male is deeper and harsher, the voice of the female is more melodious. Accordingly of the male they say عار [ʿār] arra, but of the female زمر [zamara] zamara, which is to sing. And the female's voice itself is called زمار [zimār] zimar, or song. 3. Ostriches are rightly said to exult in their wings, since their swiftness depends wholly on their wings: for although these are useless to them for flight, yet they help them wonderfully in running, and are like sails on a ship. This ancient and modern writers report by common consent. Xenophon, Anabasis (Cyrus the Younger), book 1: Στρουθὸν δὲ οὐδεὶς ἔλαβεν, etc. Πολὺ γὰρ ἀπέσπα ὑποφεύγουσα, τοῖς μὲν ποσὶ δρόμῳ, ταῖς δὲ πτέρυξιν ἄρασα, ὥσπερ ἱστίῳ χρωμένη [Strouthon de oudeis elaben, etc. Poly gar apespa hypopheugousa, tois men posi dromō, tais de pteryxin arasa, hōsper histiō chrōmenē]. No one caught an ostrich, etc. For in flight it drew far away, running with its feet, but raised by its wings and using them as a sail. Diodorus, book 3: Ὅταν κατ᾽ ἀνέμου πνοὰς ἐξαίρῃ τὰς πτέρυγας ὑπερεξάγει καθαπερεί τις ναῦς ἱστιοδρομοῦσα [Hotan kat᾽ anemou pnoas exairē tas pterygas hyperexagei kathaperei tis naus histiodromousa]; When it raises its wings with a following wind, it is carried like a ship under full sail. And shortly after: Ὅταν δὲ ἐν νηνεμίᾳ διώκηται, ταχὺ συνιδρουσῶν τοῦ πτερύγων ἀδυνατεῖ χρήσασθαι τοῖς τῆς φύσεως προτηρήμασιν, καὶ ῥᾳδίως καταλαμβανόμενον ἁλίσκεται [Hotan de en nēnemia diōkētai, tachy synidrousōn tou pterygōn adynatei chrēsasthai tois tēs physeōs protērēmasin, kai rhadiōs katalambanomenon haliksetai]; But when they pursue the animal in a calm, its wings soon become soaked with sweat, and since it cannot use its natural defences, they overtake it without any trouble and catch it. Aelian, book 2, chapter 27: Ἡ στρουθὸς ἡ μεγάλη λασίοις μὲν τοῖς πτεροῖς ἐπτέρωται [Hē strouthos hē megalē lasiois men tois pterois epterōtai].
